verdict: OK to lend selectively in Bhubaneswar IT-enabled services & BPO — pursue captive/GCC-linked and domestic-process mid-size operators with contracted receivables; avoid small voice-only exporters with single-client dependence and thin equity.
title: Bhubaneswar IT-enabled services & BPO: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**An IT-enabled services or BPO unit in Bhubaneswar sells trained seats and process hours, not products.** Cash comes in as monthly invoices to clients, mostly overseas, and goes out as salaries, rent and telecom. The asset base is light — desktops, leasehold fit-out, and a leased floor — so the real collateral is receivables and the promoter's equity, not plant. **Pricing power is weak in voice-only work and stronger in specialised analytics or captive support** [9].

## Where cash and value sit
**Value sits in the client contract and the trained bench; cash sits in receivables.** The working-capital cycle is short in principle but stretches when a single client pays late, and growth consumes cash because salaries are paid before invoices are collected [11]. Capex is modest per seat but lumpy when a new floor is taken. **So when a proposal lands, check the top-client share and the receivable ageing first; if one client is above a third of revenue, ask for the contract term and payment history.**

## What has changed now
**The state is building for scale: a planned 4.5M sq ft IT park at Bhubaneswar to absorb a $5.25 billion tech pipeline of GCCs, BPO operators, semiconductors and data centres** [1], sited near Damana Square [2]. Separately, Bhubaneswar is reported to have added over 70 companies in the last seven years [3] — treat that as local press, not audited data. Peer results are mixed: eClerx revenue rose 17.1% YoY to INR 1,212.6 crore [5], while Hinduja Global Solutions revenue grew only 1.1% YoY with EBITDA margin at 11.2% against 19.0% [6]. Large IT held margins, TCS at 24% and Infosys at 21% [7]. **Read this as: demand exists, but margin is being competed away at the small end.**

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
**Pursue mid-size operators with two or more paying clients, a domestic or GCC-anchored contract, and promoter equity already in the business.** Avoid pure voice exporters with one client and no second line of revenue. Structure as a working-capital line against receivables with a charge on current assets, plus a term loan only for fit-out matched to the lease. **Take monthly: receivable ageing, client-wise billing, employee count and attrition, and bank statements of the operating account.** Covenant on top-client concentration and on debt-service cover; if concentration rises, ask for a client diversification plan before enhancing limits.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for salary delays, rising unbilled revenue, and a falling seat count against billed seats.** If receivables beyond 90 days cross a fifth of the book, stop enhancement and reprice. If attrition or a client notice appears, ask for the replacement pipeline. **The data pack gives no city score [D], so this call rests on first principles and peers, not a local index.**
watch: Over 90-day receivables above a fifth of book -> freeze enhancement and reprice
Single client above a third of revenue -> ask for diversification plan before any limit increase
Employee count vs billed seats and attrition (monthly)
Seat count falling against billing -> ask for client pipeline and review limits
Salary payment delays or overdraft use -> escalate to credit head and reassess
